title: Money and the teaching
tomorrow: a paycheck in four parts. which parts, and why?

cards: A first paycheck has its own feel: the number is small, and it's all yours. Then a little guilt can creep in, for anyone who's picked up the idea that a spiritual person shouldn't want money. So, on this path, is it okay?
The Buddha's answer to a wealthy householder named Anathapindika is a list of happinesses. And the first one on it is having money.

teach.b: He names four kinds of happiness for someone who lives at home. The happiness of having: wealth gained by effort, by the strength of your arms and the sweat of your brow, earned rightly.
The happiness of using it, for yourself, your family and doing good. The happiness of owing nothing. And the happiness of blamelessness: knowing your work and your life do no wrong.

teach.h: BLAMELESS: WORTH MORE THAN ALL THREE.
teach.b: That last one, this sutta says, is worth far more than the other three together. So the answer is yes, with a shape. Money isn't the enemy, and wanting it isn't either.
What matters is how it came and what it does.
Rightly earned is the hinge. And notice who he says it to: not a monk, but a householder with a business to run.

teach.h: THE WHOLE WEEK IN ONE LINE.
teach.b: And that's the whole last week in one line. Work where you are. Honest work.
Effort tuned. Kind words. Duties both ways.
Earned like that, money comes with the happiness that's worth the most: nothing to hide.

how: Lay Buddhists are taught to earn a living rightly and to use wealth for family, friends and giving, and AN 4.62 is one of the suttas teachers turn to on money.

games.q: what does “money and the teaching” mean?
o: money matters more than how it was made
wealth is praised when it's rightly earned
a spiritual person should own nothing

games.q: the four happinesses — tap the pairs.
p: for yourself, your family, and good
worth more than the other three

s: Buddhism teaches that wanting money is always wrong
for people living at home, the Buddha praised wealth rightly earned and used well.
the sutta says blamelessness is worth more than having, using and owing nothing
those three are real happinesses; blamelessness outweighs them.
the sutta praises wealth however it was gained
rightly earned is the hinge: by effort, without wrong.

games.q: your cousin got a big bonus by fudging sales numbers. he says the Buddha praised wealth, so it's fine. what fits AN 4.62?
o: it praises wealth rightly earned; fudged numbers miss the hinge.
he's right; the sutta praises wealth, so the bonus counts.
no wealth is praised at all; the sutta says give it all away.
games.why: the happiness of having is for wealth rightly earned, and blamelessness is worth more than the other three. how it came is the point.

practice: Count on your fingers what you have enough of right now: a meal today, a place to sleep, someone who'd pick up if you called, a pair of shoes. Stop when you run out of fingers or things, and rest on the word enough.

wordCard.voice: Money and the teaching: wealth isn't the enemy. Rightly earned and used well, it's praised, and blamelessness is worth the most.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: dhana, wealth; AN 4.62 praises wealth gained rightly.

carryVoice: Keep this one: rightly earned, so there's nothing to hide when you count it. Seven of fifty.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 4.62, Anana Sutta (to Anathapindika: the happiness of having, of using, of debtlessness, and of blamelessness; wealth gained by effort, strength of arm and sweat of brow, righteously gained; blamelessness worth more than the other three)
